Title: Traffic and Ant Allocation Lab
Summary: Build a deadline calculator for known disjoint routes and expose why permanently reserving the first shortest path can lose.
Overview:
Build an allocation calculator for a supplied set of internally vertex-disjoint start-to-end paths. It finds the smallest completion deadline supported by those paths and constructs a valid pipeline. Then compare two supplied route sets on a colony where a greedy shortest-path reservation performs worse.

Reuse P05's distance vocabulary and P06's movement checker. This project teaches throughput, makespan and allocation without pretending that its restricted route-set calculator solves the whole colony problem. The counterexample motivates residual rerouting in P08.

Refresher:
Makespan is the number of turns until the last ant arrives. For a path of length l edges used as a pipeline, its first ant arrives at turn l and each further ant can arrive one turn later. By deadline T it can deliver max(0,T-l+1) ants. This formula also gives T deliveries for a direct edge, respecting one use of that edge per turn.

For internally disjoint paths, sum those capacities. A deadline can carry n ants exactly when the sum is at least n. Allocate no more than each path's capacity and stop once n ants are assigned. The formula applies to the supplied independent paths; overlapping paths share rooms or edges and invalidate the simple sum.

Compare lengths [2,4] for four ants: T=3 carries 2+0, T=4 carries 3+1. Sending all four down the shortest path takes five turns. Good allocation can improve a fixed route set, but finding that set is a different problem.
Spec:
1. Implement Allocate(lengths,n) for positive path lengths and positive n. Return the minimum feasible integer deadline and counts per path, with sum counts=n.
  2. Preserve input path order for equal decisions. At the minimum deadline, allocate up to each path's deadline capacity in supplied order until all ants are assigned. Zero allocation is permitted.
  3. Use checked arithmetic and early capacity saturation at n; reject negative/zero lengths, nonpositive n and representational overflow.
  4. Build a schedule generator for explicitly supplied internally vertex-disjoint paths. Assign ant IDs by path order then launch order; advance existing ants before launching the next ant on each path. Check the result with P06.
  5. Reject overlapping ordinary rooms, duplicate path edges and malformed paths at the schedule boundary. Unlimited start/end do not authorize a duplicated direct tunnel.
  6. The CLI fixture uses lengths [2,4], n=4; print turns=4 counts=3,1.
  7. Submit a written counterexample: edges s-a, a-b, b-t, a-c, c-d, d-t, s-e, e-f, f-b. Reserving shortest s-a-b-t permanently blocks two disjoint routes s-a-c-d-t and s-e-f-b-t. For four ants, compare the shortest-only six-turn pipeline with the two-route five-turn pipeline. This demonstrates greedy failure; prove global optimality later with P11.

Components.Title: Calculate deadline capacity
Components.Goal: Translate route length into how many ants can arrive on time.
Before: Why is there a +1 in T-l+1?
How does a direct edge differ from unlimited terminal occupancy?
Steps: Write boundary tests at T=l-1, l and l+1.
Sum capacities with saturation at n to avoid needless overflow.
Search a safe interval from the shortest length to shortest length+n-1.
Components.Hint: A length-four path delivers its first ant at turn four, not turn three. Test that off-by-one before using the formula in a search.
Components.Trace: For [2,4], n=4, capacities at T=3 are [2,0]; at T=4 they are [3,1].
Components.Gate: Every returned deadline is feasible and deadline-1 is infeasible for the supplied route set.

Components.Title: Allocate ants and construct pipelines
Components.Goal: Turn counts into a legal concurrent schedule.
Before: How will an ant receive a stable ID?
Which capacity rules are already guaranteed by path disjointness?
Steps: Choose counts within capacities summing exactly to n.
Generate turns including arrivals and new launches.
Pass every generated turn to P06's independent checker.
Components.Hint: On a path s-a-t, the second turn can move the first ant to t and launch the second to a. A strict empty-at-start-of-turn rule would incorrectly slow the pipeline.
Components.Trace: For a length-two path with three ants, list arrivals at turns 2,3,4. Add one ant on a length-four path arriving at turn 4.
Components.Gate: The [2,4] fixture ends in four turns, assigns every ID once and passes the movement checker.

Components.Title: Break a greedy path reservation
Components.Goal: Separate route-set selection from allocation and motivate rerouting.
Before: Can two longer paths finish four ants sooner?
Steps: Check both length-four alternatives are internally disjoint.
Compute and simulate the two candidate plans, recording exactly what this comparison proves.
Components.Hint: Deleting a and b after selecting the first shortest path destroys both alternatives. Residual capacity later permits revising a choice rather than freezing it.
Components.Trace: Shortest-only length 3 with four ants takes 6 turns. Two length-4 routes with two ants each take 5. Do not infer this from total path lengths.
Components.Gate: Explain why a valid greedy schedule is not enough for a fewest-turns claim and preserve the graph for the P11 oracle.

Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/allocation.json
Verification:
• Lengths [2,4], n=4: turns=4, counts=[3,1].
  • Lengths [1], n=3: turns=3, counts=[3]; never three ants through the direct tunnel at once.
  • Lengths [3,3], n=4: turns=4, counts=[2,2].
  • Length zero, n zero and empty route list: error.
  • A supplied overlapping path pair: reject before using the additive capacity formula.
  • The greedy counterexample: demonstrate a legal five-turn alternative to the six-turn shortest-only plan.

Exit gate

For each result, show feasibility at T and infeasibility at T-1 within the fixed route set. Explicitly state that this calculator is not a general minimum-turn colony solver.
Engineering: Why does minimum total walking distance differ from minimum last-arrival time?
What assumptions make the sum of route capacities valid?
How can one shortest path prevent a better collection of longer paths?
Does maximizing the number of disjoint routes by itself minimize completion time?
When is a zero allocation to a valid route the right decision?
What independent evidence would be needed to call the counterexample's five-turn plan globally optimal?
How does the direct-tunnel case expose a common terminal-capacity misunderstanding?
Practical: Trace capacities at the two neighboring deadlines for [2,4].
Change n from 4 to 5 and recompute.
Test a single direct edge with three ants.
Draw the greedy counterexample and label consumed ordinary rooms.
Pass a generated pipeline through P06.
Add an overlapping route test that would fool a length-only calculator.
Extras: Add a capacity table export for every searched deadline. Make off-by-one errors visible.
Add binary search over the monotone fixed-route capacity function and compare probe counts.
Allow a documented path priority while retaining stable tie-breaking.
Build a visualization-free text timeline of launches and arrivals for review.
